entities.summary:
Werner von Steußlingen, Archbishop of Mainz from 1109 to 1151 and Imperial Chancellor, emerged as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in the fragmented landscape of the Holy Roman Empire during the early 12th century. Born around 1050, his exceptionally long tenure spanned a period of profound transition following the Investiture Controversy, positioning him as a crucial mediator and power broker. His influence extended across Western Europe, particularly in German lands, where he navigated complex relations between the Salian dynasty, the emerging Hohenstaufen, and the papacy, shaping both religious practice and the political trajectory of the Empire.

His archiepiscopate was marked by intense political maneuvering and significant religious administration. Werner's election to Mainz in 1109 was contentious, occurring amidst the ongoing struggle between Emperor Henry IV and his son Henry V, and requiring papal confirmation. He consistently supported Emperor Henry V in the final stages of the Investiture Controversy, playing a role in the lead-up to the Concordat of Worms in 1122, which partially resolved the dispute over episcopal appointments. Following the death of Henry V, Werner initially supported Lothair III but later became a staunch advocate for Conrad III, helping secure his election as King of the Romans in 1138 and supporting his imperial policy against the Welf faction. He consecrated the new Mainz Cathedral in 1137, a testament to his spiritual leadership and administrative prowess.
